title: Equilibrium Constants in Terms of Partition Functions
lead: Statistical mechanics can give an equilibrium constant without any calorimetry. Writing each species' chemical potential through its molecular partition function and asking where the Helmholtz energy stops changing leads to a formula for K built from molecular data, which a worked example applies to hydrogen chloride.
notes: Adapted from the Wikibooks Statistical Thermodynamics and Rate Theories page under CC BY-SA 4.0; its plot of the Helmholtz energy against the equilibrium shift, linked from Wikimedia Commons, is not shown.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise is new and AI-written, with an AI solution checked by computation.

exercises.source_id: The spontaneity of this reaction is largely due to the electronic partition function
exercises.prompt: In Example 26.8.1 the electronic factor of $K_c$ for H2 + Cl2 ⇌ 2HCl is $e^{(2D_0(\mathrm{HCl}) - D_0(\mathrm{H_2}) - D_0(\mathrm{Cl_2}))/RT}$, with the table's $D_0$ of 427.7, 431.9 and 239.0 kJ/mol. Evaluate it (a) at 650 K and (b) at 1000 K, and say why $K_c$ falls as the temperature rises.

answer.solution:
The bonds formed beat the bonds broken by $2(427.7) - 431.9 - 239.0 = 184.5$ kJ/mol.

(a) At 650 K the exponent is $184\,500/(8.314 \times 650) = 34.14$, so the factor is $e^{34.14} = 6.7 \times 10^{14}$.

(b) At 1000 K the exponent is $184\,500/(8.314 \times 1000) = 22.19$, so the factor is $e^{22.19} = 4.3 \times 10^{9}$.

The other three ratios change only slowly with $T$, so $K_c$ follows the electronic factor. Its exponent is $D_0$'s difference over $RT$, and a larger $RT$ shrinks the advantage of the stronger bonds: the reaction is exothermic, and its $K_c$ falls as it is heated.

footnotes.html: The subscript $N_{j\neq 1}$ means $N_{j\neq i}$: every number of molecules except that of species $i$ is held constant.

The table's $\Theta_\nu$ are swapped: 6125 K belongs to H$_2$ and 808 K to Cl$_2$. The masses in the translational factors are not those of the molecules (HCl is $6.054 \times 10^{-26}$ kg, not $2.1957 \times 10^{-24}$ kg, and likewise for H$_2$ and Cl$_2$), and the final product puts H$_2$'s translational factor in the numerator and takes the rotational ratio $(42.76)^2/((3.71)(925.9))$ as 0.1333 instead of 0.532. With the true masses and the table's own $\Theta_r$, $\Theta_\nu$ and $D_0$, the four ratios are 28.4 (translation), 0.532 (rotation), 0.713 (vibration) and $6.70 \times 10^{14}$ (electronic), so $K_c = 7.2 \times 10^{15}$ at 650 K rather than $2.26 \times 10^{11}$. The conclusion stands: the electronic factor dominates.

steps.cap: The logarithm of a quotient is a difference, $\ln(x^N/y) = N\ln x - \ln y$, and $k_B\kT$ is a constant at fixed $\kT$.

steps.tex: \mk{m}{\kmui} = \mk{k}{-k_B\kT}\left[\mk{q}{\left(\dfrac{\partial N_i\ln \kqi(\kV,\kT)}{\partial N_i}\right)} - \mk{n}{\left(\dfrac{\partial (N_i\ln N_i - N_i)}{\partial N_i}\right)}\right]_{\kT,\kV,N_{j\neq i}}

steps.cap: $\kqi$ depends on $\kV$ and $\kT$ only, so $\partial(N_i\ln \kqi)/\partial N_i = \ln \kqi$; by the product rule $\partial(N_i\ln N_i)/\partial N_i = \ln N_i + 1$.
A difference of logarithms is the logarithm of the quotient.
